fragment: Got your car note in my cup
annotation:
Lean, a popular drug drink in Hip Hop Culture, is a mix of promethazine and codeine cough syrup   with jolly ranchers and sprite that give it sweetness and the trademark purple color. The drink is typically on ice, stirred never shaken and served in a double styrofoam cup. Back in the day, Actavis was a key lean ingredient. It has been discontinued due to Hip-Hop’s popularization of the drug and it’s misuse. 2 Chainz raps about how he still has some bottles of “Act” left in his cabinets in his hit Watch Out. Actavis makes lean super expensive. A typical pint of the cough syrup Actavis can cost between $250 to $400. In Houston, the birthplace of lean, a pint can sell for up to $1,000, and in Atlanta, pints have been reportedly sold for $1,200.

A car note is your car payment. The average monthly car payment is about 500 dollars. 2 Chainz sips lean that costs twice that amount on the regular.

fragment:

 Square with the stamp, for Kevin Durant
annotation:
A “square” denotes a brick, with a price “stamp” of “Kevin Durant”, who has the jersey number 35. This means Gucci Mane is selling bricks for $3500. Durant had his number 35 while playing for the Oklahoma City Thunders and carried it over to the Golden State Warriors.

Notice the play on ‘point,’ as scoring points are the main focus of the sport of basketball.

fragment:
Came in the game gettin’ money
 Flippin’ chickens, whip it, gettin’ money
annotation:
50 came into the rap game hot off the block. Get Rich or Die Tryin' was his studio debut, and sold 8.1 million copies—one of the most profitable rap albums of all time.

However, 50 was already making money before he started making a name for himself. “Flippin' chickens” means selling cocaine (e.g. “birds”). 50 was an active drug dealer from the age of 12, right up to the beginning of his music career.

Virgil’s designs often incorporate the labeling of items that don’t need to be, such as “shoelaces,” like on his rendition of the Nike Air Jordan 1 or his own 2.0 Low-Top OFF-WHITEs.



Westside Gunn and Conway the Machine respectively all implore the designer to label their “bricks” of cocaine. This may suggest that Griselda’s supply is so exclusive that it is touched by high-end fashion designers, as well inferring that the trio is bringing high fashion to the streets.

I’m a fashion, art guy. I’m always just thinking wild. Virgil always writing “Shirt” or “Sneakers” on sneakers, so I just wanted him to write “Brick” on my brick. No lie, when I made that part, I just knew that was gonna really get Virgil. Virgil already been tapped in like me and Virgin already DMed each other mad times, and you he’d been a fan since FLYGOD album, he posted songs off FLYGOD. I already knew he was tapped in and we rock a lot of OFF-WHITE shit all the time, so it always been love with Virgil.

– Westside Gunn, Rap Radar

On Twitter, Virgil responded to the reference by tweeting “‘DONE DEAL’” as well as labeling bricks with “BRICK,” as requested:

fragment:
I got bricks and birds for retail (Ayy)
 I got 100,000 worth of belts (Racks)
annotation:
If you’re selling cocaine (bricks and birds) or drugs in general for retail price, you’re someone who buys in bulk from the main source and sells in smaller amounts for a higher price, in order to make more money.

A kilo or brick of cocaine from Colombia would cost on average between $1,500-$2,000 (wholesale) while its equivalent would sell for $30,000 (retail) in NYC. The price Thug sells his cocaine for has people asking questions about its purity and how/where he got it because the price is so high/on point.

fragment: If you got sixteen, you can get a bizzird
annotation: A bird is a kilogram of cocaine. Pimp C sells them for $16,000. The -izz- is inserted, matching “sizzurp” in the next line.

He claims to purchase kilos of cocaine for $16,500, although he has varied this figure to 17.5 and 19.5.  U.S.D.A. is Jeezy’s rap group United Streets Dopeboyz of America with Slick Pulla, Blood Raw, and other Jeezy associates.

Pimp C would later release an interlude and song in 2013 titled “16.5” where he said that price was too high and implied Jeezy wasn’t big enough in Atlanta to even get that price for a kilo of cocaine.

fragment: Even eleven-five if I see ya keep it comin’
annotation:
Possibly a double entendre:

“11-5,” as well as “11-500,” is cited by some sources as a slang term originating in the Bay Area for heroin as well as other narcotics, coming from an Oakland police code used in the 1980s-90s, and later becoming the namesake for the San Francisco hip-hop group 11/5. (cit. 1 2 3) This etymology is dubious, however, as no present day police code dictionary I was able to find lists either code for anything drug related.

Multiple Bay Area rap songs use the term, though ambiguity exists over whether it refers to heroin as claimed in the above sources or drugs more generally.

See:


I’m up the block with mark doin' knots
As I think about the hash that I just got from Josh
Pass it to dump, said “Let’s get blunted”
He said, “Ooh, that look like eleven five hundred”
What do you mean? That’s hash, you fool
Mac Dre, “Let’s Go Riden”

Rocks jumpin off marijuana and herb
Eleven five hundreds due, dope fiends due off that dog food
E-40, “On a Mission”

I’m the guy he talkin' about when he say, he know a guy
Sellin' that there Qaddafi, that eleven five
E-40, “I Know A Guy”

From the land of the crooks and thieves, eleven-five, dogfood and cha-cha
E-40, “Up or Down”


Usages of the term in music outside of the Bay exist but are similarly ambiguous:


Eleven five that torture
Look what the bundle man done brought'cha
Prime Time, “Do Ya Really Wanna”

Out the mud with the drugs, now we gotta race car
Eleven five on the side, I ain’t took a day off
Kevin Gates,

fragment:
I done seen Hercules run
 We was powerlifting 2.2's
annotation:
Powerlifters usually lift hundreds of pounds on the bench press, deadlifts and squats, but the Clipse summoned the strength of Hercules during their days of drug distribution as they moved heavy weight in the form of kilograms of cocaine.

Although the weight of a kilo equals 2.2 pounds, the power of Pusha and Malice in the dope game was lifted while others who appeared just as strong couldn’t handle the weight and ran for the exit.

annotation: A key (or “ki”) is slang for a kilogram, usually referring to cocaine. Malice takes his kilos of coke and breaks them down into $10 dime bags that usually contain one gram of dope that sells to the fiends as much as candy like Gobstoppers being sold to kids.

fragment: Got some redbones to go out to Phoenix, get that Amare
annotation:
A redbone is a ruddy, light-skinned black girl. In the classic meme of a sexy girl transporting drugs for a rapper, Jeezy has his redbone go to Arizona to buy him cocaine

Jeezy refers to cocaine here as “Amare”, referring to basketball player Amar'e Stoudemire, whose number is 1. This is a play on Jay-Z’s celebrated line:

If Jeezy’s paying Lebron I’m paying Dwayne Wade

Jeezy is saying that if Jay-Z pays $3K for a kilo of cocaine (a ridiculously low number), then he pays $1K!

You know what guys? How about this? I get people to PAY ME to take their cocaine? How about that? Are there any basketball players with negative numbers?!

fragment: Hood Pope, I’m like a reverend, teeth is worth a kilo
annotation:
Ferg references his August 2013 track, “Hood Pope,” where he gave himself the eponymous title:

Ohh, this the Hood Pope
Chain hang low, red rubies and the gold
Ohh, young Trap Lord
Feel your pain, I be down for my people

Ferg has a custom made grill with the moniker laid out in multi-colored diamonds and rubies, which was inspired by a photo he’d seen of the pope with a jewel-encrusted crucifix.  He paid $10,000 for the grill, not quite on par with the 2019 price of a kilogram of cocaine, which typically ranges between $20,000-$30,000.

fragment:
Quarter brick, half a brick, whole brick, ayy nigga
 Time to whip these zippers in the kitchen with the same nigga
annotation:
Freddie detailing the grind of whipping crack : quarter kilo, half a kilo, the whole kilo.
“Whipping zippers” refers to cooking one ounce batches at once – a “zip” being an ounce. There are 35.2 ounces in a kilogram, which means 36 batches assuming a bit of wastage. You can see where it would become tedious.

Gibbs details “the same nigga” because usually, with an operation moving kilos, the same people will cook all the time, to make the product consistent and ensure the high is within a tight margin across the brick.

He is also referencing the hook to a popular song by Gucci Mane and OJ Da Juiceman called “Make the Trap Say Aye” :

Quarter-brick, half a brick
Whole brick, aye!
Quarter-pound, half a pound
Whole pound, ok!

fragment: Gettin’ that chicken with blue cheese, yeah
annotation:
Taken literally, putting blue cheese on chicken is  pretty bougie, but chicken is also slang for a kilo of coke, and blue cheese refers to the blue stripe featured on $100 bills as an anti-counterfeit method.  He wants more than just expensive food…



The food reference ties back to Quavo’s “Ratatouille” line, as both of these rappers are in the kitchen cooking.

fragment: Give me a pistol, then run with the K’s
annotation:
Ace Hood is assuring you even with just a pistol (a small firearm) that he could hold his own in an environment where every other goon has a ‘K’, which is a slang name for an “AK-47”, an automatic assault rifle much more deadly than a handgun.



K’s could also be referring to a kilo(gram) of cocaine- approximately 2.2 pounds of weight. This double entendre suggest that in the drug industry you don’t need any significant weaponry to manage to make it back home safe.

fragment: That’s why I hustle for half a key, that’s twelve G’s (G)
annotation:
Following up on from the previous line, Ross explains he sells cocaine in order to let his mother retire comfortably, as he was tired of watching her struggle.

In Miami, a kilo of coke is worth of 20K-28.5K, so when Ross is selling $12K for a half a kilo, he might be asking for too much.

annotation: G-wagon is the nickname given to the vehicles in the Mercedes Benz G class. 10 days before Major Key dropped, Rick Ross actually bought a G65 that costs $230k.

fragment:
I got them keys, the keys, the keys

 I got them keys, the keys, the keys

A reference to DJ Khaled’s phrase “I got the keys to more success,” which is Khaled’s way of sharing advice, or news, used on his snapchat. The hook is doubly relevant, with Khaled’s recent signing to Roc-A-Fella and the symbolic gifting of Jay Z’s last original Roc-A-Fella chain.

A key is short for kilograms  of cocaine. A kilo contains 2.2 pounds, usually for distribution.

Jay Z also has a storied history of selling cocaine, learning his unique business skills from pushing white powder.

Additionally, the music video shows black prisoners locked up by white police officers.  Khaled and Future might hope to free these oppressed individuals through their influence of money.

fragment:
Studio right in my yaad
 I’m doin’ ten in a week
annotation:
Although Drake’s pronunciation makes the lyric sound like “yacht,” it’s actually “yaad.” “Yaad” is a Jamaican slang for a person’s home. Drake makes ten songs at his home per week.

In an interview with Genius, Allen Ritter, a close collaborator with Drake, stated that “Work” was made at Drake’s house:

Drake had this pool party the day before we were all out there. […] He told us we can stay there to make music at his house. Sevn pulled the “Work” beat, but nobody knew where to take it. As soon as he pulled that up, I played the keys on it. I honestly didn’t even think the beat was done. But it’s big now.

The YOLO Estate doesn’t have a confirmed studio within the house or yard, however, at an estimated price tag of $20 million with 12,500 square feet, it’s likely Drake has one set up.

fragment:
All these record labels broke as shit
 Ricky Dinky record shit
annotation:
Rinky Dinky Records is a reference to Project Pat’s skits on his Ghetty Green album, on which he and Three 6 Mafia make fun of broke labels trying to sign them with weak offers, such as offering $7000 and a new fridge.

Gucci already owns his imprint, 1017 Brick Squad Records, under the umbrella of Warner Music Group, so no need to waste time with such ridiculous offers.

fragment: Got Pradas every color and I got CCs you ain’t seen yet
annotation:
NAV is rocking some exclusive Chanel sneakers, which feature the brands iconic “interlocking Cs” logo on the side. Chanel’s menswear line is unable to be purchased from the brand’s online store and subsequently can only be acquired by visiting one of their brick and mortar locations. Furthermore, Chanel shoes are comparatively very expensive in contrast to a sportswear brand such as Nike or adidas. Whilst an average pair of sneakers tends to cost approximately $75, the low-top iteration of Chanel’s SS18 sneakers costs a hefty $880.



NAV has rapped about his love of Chanel sneakers before in his music. He used a similar line on his 2018 track “Champion”, which coincidentally also featured Travis Scott, where he rapped:

Two Cs on my shoes, these not no ASICS

The term “bird” was at its height during the 1990s/2000s Mafioso rap trend but has since died down.

fragment:

annotation:
These lines mark the end of Jay ranting about the negative aspects of fame, making sure that he’s “not going too far with the complaints” because he does have a good life.

Of the material perks he enjoys is a 5 kilogram cuban link chain, and a $500,000 Maybach 62, complete with window curtains to block out paparazzi. He previously mentioned the ride in “30 Something”:

I got that six-deuce with curtains, so you can’t see me / And I didn’t even have to put tints on it

fragment: If Jeezy’s payin’ LeBron, I’m payin’ Dwyane Wade
annotation:
JAY-Z flips the hook of Jeezy’s 2009 song “24-23”:

See I used to pay Kobe, but now I pay Lebron
Kobe, Lebron, Kobe, Lebron

Jeezy uses Kobe and Lebron’s jersey numbers from the 2009-2010 NBA season (24 and 23) as an analogy for the drug game—he used to pay $24,000 for a kilo of cocaine, but now he only shells out $23,000.

So while Jeezy bragged about paying $23,000 for a kilo of cocaine, Jay takes this a step further, claiming that he can get a kilo of coke for Dwyane Wade’s jersey number, which is 3.

fragment:
Turn that sixty-two to one-twenty-five, one-twenty-five to a two-fifty
 Two-fifty to a half a— Man, ain’t nothin’ nobody can do with me
annotation:
Referring to cocaine weights and the money made from selling it: 62 grams = 1/16 kilo, 125 grams = 1/8 kilo, 250 grams = ¼ kilo, 500 grams = ½ kilo. Jay-Z is one of the richest people in rap. He’s known for doubling his dollars, legally and illegally!

Then, he turns the 250 from grams into dollars (rhetorically), and doubles it (i.e. $250,000 to $500,000). He slurs “half a million” so it sounds like “half a man.”

This might also be referring to Jay-Z’s net worth over the years. He’s now worth over half a billion ($650 million)

This is also a nice follow-up to “The Bounce” from The Blueprint 2, in which he raps “I turn a 8 to an ounce to a whole key to the R.O.C.”

BUT COULDN’T IT BE “HALF A MAN”?
“half a man” could be a metaphor for a half a brick. You can’t pull a half-a-million-dollar flip off of 250 grams of cocaine, but Jay could be talking about heroin in these lines. The term “boy” is used as code for heroin. And Jay has talked horse before: on the seven-minute freestyle with Big L, Jay says, “I cause vials to move when I come creeping through your way with a 1000 little dudes.” 1000 little dudes = a key of heroin, or a boy. And what is half a man but a boy? Again, heroin in general is often called boy; “How lil dude boxing?” or “Lil dude flow decent?” are codes for “Was that batch of boy straight?”

Meek Mill uses a similar line in “Get Dis Money”.

fragment:
I would’ve took a hundred million and gave twenty to Hov
 I heard it’s the way they did it when we only had the stove
annotation:
Apple’s deal with Drake was allegedly worth $19 million. Ye is claiming his earning potential is 5 times that. During Jay’s “Tidal Freestyle” he claimed:

Jimmy Iovine offered a safety net

During the tortured launch of Tidal there were rumours that Iovine attempted to lure artists away from the service with Apple Music deals. Ye seems to confirm this, although his price may have been too high.

“Stove” is a play on words with “Tim Cook,” as well as a reference to Jay Z’s drug dealing past. On the very first Roc-A-Fella track Kanye is featured on, “The Bounce”, Jay raps:

 I turn a 8 to an ounce
To a whole ki to the R.O.C

 Jay turns a small amount of cocaine, through cooking it and cutting, into an ounce of crack, which he flips to re-up, eventually turning it to a kilo. Kanye recognises the work Jay put in to his own career, and offers to “cut” Jay in on the deal. The $20 million may also be to smooth over any hard feelings if Ye decided against going with Tidal.

fragment:
Now the Nets a stone throw from where I used to throw bricks
 So it’s only right I’m still tossin’ ’round Knicks, ugh
annotation:
Hov is referencing his crack cocaine stash spot at 560 State Street in Boerum Hill, Brooklyn. Hov bought apartment 10B in the early-90’s, and lived there with B-High and Ty Ty.

As you can see in the photo below, the Barclays Center, which is the home of basketball’s Brooklyn Nets and an arena Hov is an investor in, is just a stones throw away from Hov’s old pad. Each and every event held at the Barclays will add to Hov’s net profits as a part-owner.



Hov buries a few more basketball and drug-dealing references here:


Of course, the New York Knicks are a NBA team; and one of the Nets biggest rivals seeing they are both New York City-based teams. Hov hopes when they meet that his Nets will toss around the Knicks, that is, beat them in the “Battle of the Boroughs.”
He and his crew would turn cocaine bricks into crack rocks, or stones, and then sell them to the public. On the street you can buy a nickel bag, known as a “nick,” for $5. Hov was selling nicks in the form of crack then; now he still sells product, but in the form of singles and albums.
“Throwing a brick” in basketball is a missed shot that hits the rim and bounces off. Luckily for Hov the shots thrown from his [k]nicks weren’t bricks, but rather left his customers happy and had him flushed with cash.

fragment:
And your homeboy need subpoena, that predator move in flocks
 That name gotta be registered and placed on neighborhood watch
annotation:
Lamar doubles down on his allegation that Drake is a pedophile. Sex offenders are, via Megan’s Law, legally required to be publicly identifiable to their local community in the U.S. This line embodies the cover art of the song, as it displays a Google Earth screenshot of Drake’s $100 million dollar Toronto mansion photoshopped onto a sex offender app GPS with various pings over the estate:



The mansion, dubbed “The Embassy” by Drake, was the exact estate he suggested would be raided for sex crimes in his May 2024 diss track “meet the grahams:”

The Embassy ‘bout to get raided, too, it’s only a matter of time

Prior to that, Kendrick called Drake a predator and implied that Drake ran a sex trafficking ring of sorts in his home:

And we gotta raise our daughters knowin' there’s predators like him lurkin'
[…]
It’s some weird shit goin' on and some of these artists be here to police it
They be streamlinin' victims all inside of they home and callin' ‘em tender
Then leak videos of themselves to further push their agendas

The homeboy needing subpoena likely refers to OVO signee Baka Not Nice, who was arrested for sex trafficking and assault in June 2014.

The word “flocks” could be another reference to birds, as a group of birds is often called a “flock.” This is in addition to previous lines in the song where Kendrick uses the word “foul” as a homophone for fowl:

Did Cole foul, I don’t know why you still pretendin’

He also compares members of OVO, whose logo is an owl, to bir

fragment: And a bird and ten grand’s where a mothafucka stand
annotation:
A “bird” is slang for a brick of cocaine, which is equal to 1 kilogram or about 36 ounces of cocaine.

One brick of cocaine is worth about $10,000, which is all many have to their name.

The line is also a nod to Kendrick’s opening lines in verse 2, as both reference lyrics from Ice Cube’s “A Bird In The Hand”, which part II of this song’s instrumental is also a nod to. Whereas Kendrick references the opening line, MC Eiht references the last line of his verse.

Cause we don’t want a drug push
But a bird in the hand, is worth more than a Bush

Both this line and Ice Cube play on the expression a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush, which means it’s better to have a guaranteed smaller success than to risk all on a bigger success that might not come through.

fragment:
Dodged a policeman, workin’ for his big homie
 Small-time hustler, graduated to a brick on him
annotation:
It’s customary for drug dealers to start off selling small amounts of product at the street level before dealing with larger amounts. “Brick” and "bird” are slang terms for a kilogram of cocaine and they go for $16,000 — $24,000.

The phrase “graduated to a brick” was originally used by Jay Z in “My 1st Song.”

fragment: Came up in my hood selling fifties like Slim Shady (Fifty)
annotation:
It’s unclear what the rationale behind this line is, but I have three ideas:

1) Refers to how Eminem (aka. Slim Shady) sold more than 50 million album copies over his career.

2) Refers to how Eminem is in his fifties.

3) Refers to Eminem’s long-term fellow rapper 50 Cent with whom he has a close relationship.

Maybe Dolph is so clever that it’s all three!

I’m unsure what kind of “fifties” Dolph is selling, but I assume it’s either album sales (50 thousand copies) or narcotics (50 pounds/kilos of something).

fragment:
I caught a sucker dyin’ ’cause he thought he could rhyme
 Now if his momma is a quarter, daughter must be a dime
annotation:
The Outkast boys have previously addressed phony rappers who deal dope as a front to selling their music, and “dyin” as a result. From their song Mainstream:

Think it is when it ain’t all peaches and cream
That’s why some are found floating face down in the mainstream

Andre addresses the “sucker” with a triple-entendre line, bringing the mama and sister into the mix. From the same song:

Cocaine dealers walk the wrong side
Up in they rides
Looking cleaner then I seen them the last time
Then selling dimes, now its quarter ki’s, stacking G’s

Andre is implying that the “sucker”, who died from pretending to be a dope dealer, was probably so desperate he would sell-out out his own family to help his rap career– pimpin' them out $25 and $10 apiece.

Additionally, he uses a play-on-words in referring to the “sucker’s” mama as a “quarter”, or “courter”, in that she’s flirtatious– and it follows that the apple doesn’t fall far from the tree.

The term “dime”, as in “dime-piece”, refers to a woman who rates 10 out of 10. If the mama is a 25 which rates way beyond a perfect 10/10, chances are her daughter better be a 10.

fragment:
Made a brick through a brick, ain’t whip up shit
 This pure cocaine, yeah
annotation:
Lil Baby is referring to selling cocaine, which is often compacted into one kilogram bricks for ease of distribution. Similarly, a brick of money refers to 1,000 bills of any denomination. A brick of hundred-dollar bills would be worth $100,000.

Baby specifies he isn’t selling crack, an adulterated form of the drug made by whipping baking soda and water with the cocaine.

fragment:
Buck, he from Cashville, Ten-a-key nigga
 We getting them ten a ki’, save ten for me nigga
annotation:
During the recording of this album, (Beg for Mercy), Tony Yayo was sentenced to prison, which is when Young Buck stepped in and joined G-Unit.

Young Buck stepping in for this album instead of the original member (Tony Yayo) is the reason to 50 Cent formally introducing Buck throughout this album.

Buck is from Nashville, Tennessee, hence the creation of his record label “Ca$hville”.

“Tennessee” sounds like “ten-a-key” when the syllables are broken down. The phrase “ten-a-key” is used to describe a kilo of drugs (usually cocaine) worth $10,000. 50 Cent is known for dealing drugs when he was younger therefore he wouldn’t mind $10,000 from drugs.

fragment: They gon’ go Tony Montana and cop them some Shaq at the free throws
annotation:
Tony Montana is the oft-referenced main character from the movie Scarface – a cocaine kingpin revered by many gangster rappers.

His large quantity of the drug, which is often packaged in “bricks,” can be compared to the number of bricks in former NBA star Shaquille O'Neal’s career at the free throw line. Shaq shot just 52.7% from the line during his career, and missed a whopping total of 5,317 over the twenty year span.



Montana’s involvement in organized crime also ties into the R.I.C.O. theme of the song.

fragment:
Nigga say that he gon’ rob me, put a brick on his ass
 Now every killer in my city tryna look for his ass
annotation:
A “brick” is a block of 1,000 bills of any denomination, for example, a brick of hundreds would be $100,000.

Meek is warning that if you threaten him, he’ll respond by putting a hit out on you.

fragment:
But said I ain’t ready, really I’m ready
 Really, I’m ready, I’m ready like never before
 I’ma just give you a key to my heart
 You’ll be the first that I let in the door

 They never would score
 All you was hearing about me and the women

annotation:
Before becoming intimate with Nicki, Meek wasn’t ready for a real relationship and Nicki would always see him in clubs with other women.

Rumours then broke in April 2015 that the pair were engaged after Meek bought Nicki a $500,000 ring heart-shaped ring. It seems the “key to his heart” was literal, and while it wasn’t an engagement ring, Meek explained the ring as a “present” – a token of their relationship.

fragment:
A hundred thousand for the jet, yeah that’s the flight bill
 Damn, cost four bricks to go to the LIV nigga
annotation:
LIV is a night club in Miami that plays host to a plethora of rap stars, including Meek on a regular basis.

LIV nightclub is located in Miami, and Meek is currently looking to reside in Hollywood, about 4 hours away. Chartering a private jet for the flight can cost up to $100,000 for a high end Gulfstream model.

A “brick” (kilo) of cocaine costs around $20,000 in the US. Meek recently revealed he made $80,000 just for a walkthrough, so an evening at LIV would net him the equivalent of four bricks of cocaine.

annotation:
Lil Durk has finally got his name out there, making hit songs and getting money. But before he became famous, he made a living off selling cocaine (“bricks”). He is also signed to Coke Boys.

In his freestyle, 52 Bars Part 2, Lil Durk claims he had $100,000 saved up before the fame.
“Sup ‘Lo, before your ass was born I saved a 100 thou”

to

You ship off keys, and we ship Grand Pianos

fragment:
Mama told me (Ayy)
 Not to sell work (Mama)
 Seventeen five, same color T-shirt (White)
 Mama told me (Ayy)
 Not to sell work (Mama)
 Seventeen five, same color T-shirt (Yeah)
annotation:
Quavo obviously didn’t listen to his mama—he’s selling work (a.k.a. drugs).

“Seventeen five” is a reference to a 2005 lyric by late Atlanta rap icon Shawty Lo, from D4L’s underground hit “I’m Da Man.” In the original song, Lo said:

And you know I keep work
Seventeen five, same color t-shirt

“Seventeen five” is a reference to cocaine prices. Buying a kilo for the low price of $17,500 implies you are high up in the drug game. Jeezy famously dubbed himself “Mr. 17.5.”

“Same color t-shirt” draws a connection between pure white cocaine and the white t-shirts that are popular with drug dealers.

fragment: Water, faucet (Splash), drippin’ off my body (Drip)
annotation:
“Water” or “ice” are popular slangs in rap music for clean jewelry and diamonds which is mostly measured in clarity.

Quavo is known to spend a lot of money on his jewelry, in April of 2017 he purchased a Napoleon chain for reportedly $35,000.



On “T-Shirt”, Takeoff used a similar line:

Neck water faucet, mockin' birds mockin' (woo)

fragment: Got bird like Birdman (Brr)
annotation: A “bird” is a brick of cocaine (2.2 pounds). Birdman is a rapper and co-founder of Cash Money Records. Although there is no proof that Baby has ever sold/bought/produced coke, he was however arrested and charged with possession of nearly a pound of marijuana in 2007.

fragment: And the keys, a piano
annotation:
A “key” is a common abbreviation for a Kilo, which equates to approximately 2.2 pounds worth of drugs and is one of the largest most used measurements when it comes to cocaine and marijuana. Also, it should be noted that cocaine is white just like the color of keys on a piano.

The Migos claim to have sold drugs before/whilst pursuing their music career in many of their songs.
 and still take a number of different narcotics to this day, so it is logical for them to reference them on a track dedicated to the lifestyle their close friends lead.



The Weeknd used a similar comparison back in 2011 on Drake’s track ““Crew Love” where he sang:

Take your nose of my keyboard,
What you bothering me for?

fragment: SRT, Redeye, red key (Vroom)
annotation:
It’s no secret that Moneybagg Yo is a fan of Dodge SRT vehicles. Within his collection, he owns a Dodge Charger SRT Hellcat Redeye. The Redeye package is equipped with an upgraded supercharger, allowing the car to reach 0-60 in as fast as 3.5 seconds.


Pictured: Moneybagg Yo standing amongst his car collection, including multiple SRTs
Since 2015, Dodge SRT vehicles come from the factory with two red keys and one black key. The black key limits the vehicle to a reduced power, while the red keys allow for full power output.

One band refers to $1,000. The name comes from the fact a band is wrapped around the wad of cash.

A plug is someone you buy drugs from. In O.T’s case, it’s likely his wholesale supplier. He buys pure bricks of cocaine, then cuts (dilutes) to sell on the streets.

fragment:
Cut it (Woo), cut it (Yeah), cut it (Baow), cut it (Go)
 Cut it (Get it), cut it (Skrrt), cut it (Bah), cut it
 Them bricks is way too hot, you need to cut it (You need to cut it)
 Your price is way too high, you need to cut it

 Your price is way too high, you need to cut it
annotation:
A brick of cocaine is one kilogram of cocaine, which costs upwards of $20,000. When a brick of cocaine is too potent (too hot) the drug dealer can dilute it with so-called cutting agents.

While this lowers the quality and purity of the cocaine, it means O.T. can sell more of his product and increase revenue. This is what he’s referring to with “your price is way too high"—selling cut cocaine (which often comes in the form of crack cocaine) is more profitable than selling pure cocaine.

O.T. Genasis is the same genius who brought us the hit song, “Coco” which shows his admiration for cocaine in the song:

I’m in love with the coco
I’m in love with the coco
I got it for the low, low

fragment:
Cut it, cut it, cut it, cut it
 Cut it, cut it, cut it, cut it
 Them bricks is way too hot, you need to cut it
 Your price is way too high, you need to cut it
annotation:
When cocaine bricks are too hot, the producer usually cuts it. When prices are too high, the buyer askes the dealer to cut the prices.

One brick of cocaine is one kilogram of cocaine, which costs upwards of $20,000. When a brick of cocaine is too potent (too hot) the drug dealer can dilute it with so-called cutting agents. This also lowers the quality and purity of the cocaine, which explains why OT is asking the dealer to lower his prices.

In another sense, kilos of coke are way too hot in terms of heat on the streets. Put simply, the vast amounts of cocaine easily attract unwanted attention. It’s too hot to have whole kilos laying around, so he should spread out his supply to divert attention.

O.T. Genasis is the same genius who brought us the hit song, “Coco” which shows his admiration for cocaine in the song.

I’m in love with the coco
I’m in love with the coco
I got it for the low, low

Street value for 36 oz (a kilogram) can range anywhere from $30,000 to $50,000.

He is also well known for Air Jordans, a brand of shoes and athletic clothing designed, owned, and produced by Nike and Michael Jordan himself. These are often referred to as “J’s”

nice word play between “stephen curry” and his jersey number “30”

 One thousand grams of cocaine, then your name will be rich
annotation:
Referencing a kilogram, or brick, of cocaine – the standard system of measurement for coke, also equivalent to 36 ounces or “zips.” A kilo can go anywhere from $15,000 to $36,000, which could be “rich” for many – at minimum wage and full-time employment (in the United States), a worker could make $15,080 a year.

A double entendre on Rich with the name of Harlem crack Dealer Rich Porter depicted in Paid In Full.

Niggas get exposed, I see the cracks and I’m the liar?
 Shit, I’ve been exposed, I took the crack and built the wire

This is a response to Drake, who questioned Pusha’s street cred on “Two Birds One Stone”:

You middle-man in this shit, boy, you was never them guys
I can tell, ‘cause I look most of you dead in your eyes

Drake was exposed for using writers in 2016 after a few reference tracks that Quintin Miller recorded for Drake songs like “10 Bands" and his verse on Meek Mill’s “R.I.C.O.” were leaked by Funk Flex during an ongoing beef between Drake and Meek.

Push came under the most scrutiny as a drug dealer when his former manager for the Clipse Tony Gonzalez was sentenced to 32 years in prison for running a “20 million dollar drug ring.”

The Wire is an HBO show based on the drug war in Baltimore. This is not the first time Pusha has mentioned the show; his debut solo album My Name Is My Name was named after a quote from the show.

Ross was 16 years old the first time he got 36 ounces (a kilogram) of cocaine. Seeing so much coke at such a young age is perhaps how he had so much money when he was only 18.

Rick Ross’s alleged drug-dealing past selling kis (kilograms) of cocaine has been part of his key to success, as well as his rap career. Now that he’s paid from slanging drugs and selling records, he can afford the keys to new cars and new houses.

In basketball terms, a “brick” is a badly missed shot that is so far off the mark it appears to have the weight of a brick.

Due to the amount or the frequency that his friend is “throwing”, or selling, bricks, Rio believes that the man could be basketball legend Shaquille O'Neal, who, with a career free-throw average of 52.7%, threw many bricks himself.

All this to say, Stove was moving a multitude of “blocks” (mostly referred to as bricks) of cocaine.

fragment: One thousand grams in a kilo

“Kilo” is short for a Kilogram.
The kilogram was originally defined as the mass of a litre (cubic decimetre) of water at its freezing point. A kilo consists of 1,000 grams as advocated by Future, most likely in reference to the cocaine mentioned in the previous line.



By the time it makes it to dealers, it’s worth maybe more like $70,000, $80,000, and by the time they cut it into grams, sometimes dilute it, a pure kilo is worth equivalent of about $150,000, so the markup is gigantic. – Tom Wainwright

fragment: 1017, that’s a brick wit’ a extra 10
annotation: Gucci’s uses his label’s name, 1017 Bricksquad, to allude to how much he’ll charge you for a brick of cocaine: $17,000.

fragment:
I left a flock of rappers dead and buried
 A verse from me is like eleven birds
 Just did the math, that’s like two thousand dollars every word
annotation:
Cole uses “flock” in conjunction with “birds,” a slang term for cocaine. This may also be a nod to the Travis, Thug, and Quavo hit, “pick up the phone,” which is the eleventh track on Travis’ September 2016 album, Birds in the Trap Sing McKnight. Coincidentally, Migos released a track titled “11 Birds” in April 2017.

Cole uses approximately 210 words on this track, including the intro and his adlibs. Therefore, according to the math, this verse costs around $420,000. Nonetheless, Cole is the executive producer of Thug’s album and likely did not charge that much, if at all.

In April 2017, Joey Bada$$ claimed that J. Cole was “done with guest features” after he appeared on Joey’s track, “LEGENDARY.” However, Cole contradicted this statement by providing twelve features in 2018. He alluded to this on 21 Savage’s December 2018 track, “a lot”:

Okay, no problem, I’ll show up on everyone album
You know what the outcome will be
I’m batting a thousand
It’s got to the point that these rappers don’t even like rappin' with me

This track is Cole’s third feature of 2019, following Offset’s “How Did I Get Here” and Ty Dolla $ign’s “Purple Emoji,” which released three days prior.

fragment: 17.5, I shave it like it’s Nair
annotation:
17.5k is the amount of money that a kilo (or 36 ounces, i.e. a bird) of cocaine sells for.

To “shave” coke is to water it down or dilute it with baby powder/baking soda/etc.

All in all, Thug compares his shaving of the coke to Nair, the hair removal product.
